title: Earning More Than Your Manager
description:
Report the `name` of every employee who earns strictly more than their own manager.

Name the column `employee`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT e.name AS employee
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
hint: Join the table to itself: one alias for the employee, one for the manager.
outputExplanation: No employee in the example data earns more than their own manager, so the result is empty. A hidden test with deeper chains produces matches.

title: Salary Rank Within Department
description:
For every employee report their salary rank inside their own department, highest salary first. Employees on equal salaries share a rank and the next rank is **not** skipped.

Name the columns `name`, `dept_id` and `rnk`. Return the result in any order.
hint: "Ties share a rank and nothing is skipped" is the definition of DENSE_RANK, as opposed to RANK.
outputExplanation: In Engineering, Ava is ranked 1st, Ben and Cara are tied at 2nd, and Dan is 3rd. In Sales, Eve is 1st, Gia is 2nd, and Finn is 3rd. Hal is the only employee in HR.

title: Above Your Department's Average
description:
Report the `name` and `salary` of every employee earning strictly more than the average salary of their own department.

Name the columns `name` and `salary`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT name, salary,
         AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_avg
  FROM employees
)
WHERE salary > dept_avg;
hint: A window AVG over PARTITION BY dept_id gives each row its department average without collapsing the rows.
outputExplanation: Ava earns more than Engineering's average of $121,250, and Eve earns more than Sales' average of $95,000. No one in HR exceeds its average.

title: Share Of Department Payroll
description:
For every employee report what percentage of their department's total payroll their own salary represents, rounded to 2 decimal places.

Name the columns `name` and `pct_of_payroll`. Return the result in any order.
hint: SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) keeps every row while giving it the department total. Multiply by 100.0, not 100, to avoid integer division.
outputExplanation: Ava accounts for 30.93% of Engineering's payroll, Ben and Cara each 24.74%, and Dan 19.59%. Eve makes up 45.61% of Sales' payroll, and Hal accounts for all of HR's.

title: Departments Paying Above Company Average
description:
Report the name of every department whose **average** salary is strictly greater than the company-wide average salary.

Name the column `department`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT d.name AS department
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
HAVING AVG(e.salary) > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);
hint: A scalar subquery in the HAVING clause is evaluated once for the whole query.
outputExplanation: Only Engineering ($121,250 average) beats the company-wide average of $103,750. Sales ($95k) and HR ($60k) fall below.

title: Top Earner Of Each Department
description:
Report the highest-paid employee of each department. If several employees tie for the top salary, report all of them.

Name the columns `department`, `name` and `salary`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT d.name AS department, e.name, e.salary
FROM (
  SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) e
JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.rnk = 1;
hint: Rank inside each department, then keep rank 1 — ties come along for free.
outputExplanation: Ava ($150k) is the top earner in Engineering, Eve ($130k) in Sales, and Hal ($60k) in HR.

title: How Many Direct Reports
description:
Report every employee who manages at least one person, together with how many **direct** reports they have.

Name the columns `manager` and `reports`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT m.name AS manager, COUNT(*) AS reports
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name;
hint: Group the self-join by the manager's id, not their name — two managers could share a name.
outputExplanation: Ava manages 3 people and Eve manages 2. No other employee manages anyone.

title: Gap To The Next Highest Salary
description:
Order all employees by salary from highest to lowest and, for each one, report how much less they earn than the person directly above them. The top earner reports `NULL`.

Name the columns `name`, `salary` and `gap`. Return the result in any order.
hint: LAG() reaches backwards one row in the window's order. Add a tie-breaker to the ORDER BY so the answer is deterministic.
outputExplanation: Ava ($150k) is the top earner and has no gap. Eve ($130k) is $20k behind Ava. Ben and Cara ($120k) follow, then Dan ($95k), Gia ($85k), Finn ($70k) and Hal ($60k).

title: Running Headcount By Hire Date
description:
Order employees by `hire_date` and report, for each hire, how many people had been hired up to and including that date.

Name the columns `hire_date`, `name` and `headcount`. Return the result in any order.
hint: A COUNT window with ORDER BY accumulates. Be explicit about the frame — ROWS and RANGE differ when dates tie.
outputExplanation: Eve was the first hire, Ava the second, Ben and Cara the third and fourth (same day), followed by Finn, Dan, Gia and Hal in order.

title: Bucket Salaries Into Bands
description:
Bucket every employee into a salary band and count each band:

- `Low` — under 80000
- `Mid` — 80000 up to but not including 130000
- `High` — 130000 and above

Employees with a NULL salary belong to the band `Unknown`. Report only bands that contain at least one employee.

Name the columns `band` and `headcount`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT CASE
         WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 'Unknown'
         WHEN salary < 80000 THEN 'Low'
         WHEN salary < 130000 THEN 'Mid'
         ELSE 'High'
       END AS band,
       COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
GROUP BY band;
hint: CASE arms are evaluated top to bottom, so test the NULL case first and let the ranges fall through.
outputExplanation: Two employees are in the High band ($130k+), four in the Mid band ($80k–$130k), and two in the Low band (under $80k). No employee has a NULL salary in this dataset.

title: Salaries Paid To More Than One Person
description:
Report every salary figure that is paid to two or more employees, along with how many people receive it.

Name the columns `salary` and `people`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT salary, COUNT(*) AS people
FROM employees
WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY salary
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
hint: GROUP BY collects NULLs into their own group — exclude them explicitly if they should not count.
outputExplanation: $120,000 is the only salary paid to more than one person — both Ben and Cara earn it. All other salaries are unique.

title: Longest-Serving Person Per Department
description:
Report the earliest-hired employee in each department. If several were hired on the same earliest date, report all of them.

Name the columns `dept_id`, `name` and `hire_date`. Return the result in any order.
hint: RANK() keeps every tied row at rank 1; ROW_NUMBER() would arbitrarily pick one.
outputExplanation: Ava (2018-01-15) is the longest-serving employee in Engineering, Eve (2017-11-02) in Sales, and Hal (2023-09-01) is the only employee in HR.

title: Hires Per Year
description:
Report how many people were hired in each calendar year.

Name the columns `year` and `hires`. Return the result in any order.
hint: strftime('%Y', date) extracts the year in SQLite; it returns text, not a number.
outputExplanation: One hire each in 2017, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023. Two hires in 2019.

title: Median Salary
description:
Report the median salary of the company: the middle value when salaries are sorted, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even. Ignore NULL salaries.

Name the column `median_salary`. The result is exactly one row.
hint: SQLite has no PERCENTILE function. Take 1 or 2 rows from the middle with LIMIT/OFFSET and average them.
outputExplanation: With 8 non-NULL salaries, the median is the average of the 4th and 5th values: $107,500.

title: Managers Of Three Or More
description:
Report the name of every manager with **three or more** direct reports.

Name the column `manager`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
hint: Same self-join as counting direct reports, with a HAVING filter on the count.
outputExplanation: Only Ava manages three or more people (3 direct reports). Eve has 2 and does not qualify.

title: Distance From Your Department's Average
description:
For every employee report how far their salary sits above or below their department's average, rounded to 2 decimals. Negative means below average.

Name the columns `name` and `diff`. Return the result in any order.
hint: Subtract the partitioned window average from the row's own salary.
outputExplanation: Ava earns $28,750 above Engineering's average, while Dan earns $26,250 below it. Eve earns $35k above Sales' average, and Finn earns $25k below. Hal is exactly at HR's average.
